# How Google thinks about crawl budget

Day 1, 16:00 · Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations · coverage: slides, transcript

The second attendee recording starts mid-talk, so the opening is from slides only.

## Claims

- **[Slide]** Google Search, Ads, Shopping and Images all request through one centralised crawling infrastructure, whose primary mandate is to fetch from the internet while strictly preventing the overloading of external servers.
  <br><sub>`D1-C066` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Crawling infrastructure](https://developers.google.com/crawling), [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extends [D1-C326](D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) · Extended by [D1-C375](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-PRF-01`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Because every Google product shares the same host capacity, Ads or Shopping fetches that hit a slow server can reduce how much is crawled for Search.
  <br><sub>`D1-C068` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget)</sub>

- **[Slide]** Crawl budget is the combination of crawl rate limit and crawl demand.
  > "Crawl Budget = Crawl Rate Limit & Crawl Demand"
  <br><sub>`D1-C090` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Used by the glossary term *Crawl budget*</sub>

- **[Slide]** Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a host-wide metric shared across all Google crawlers.
  <br><sub>`D1-C091` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D1-C374](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extended by [D1-C376](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-PRF-01`, the glossary term *Crawl rate limit (hostload)*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's crawl budget guide says each crawler has its own crawl demand, but the crawl capacity limit (hostload) is shared across all crawlers, so high demand from one crawler can reduce the capacity left for others.
  > "high demand from one crawler can reduce the capacity available for others"
  <br><sub>`D1-C132` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · is the documentation · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Used by `DEV-PRF-01`, the glossary term *Crawl rate limit (hostload)*</sub>

- **[Slide]** Hostload is driven by changes in connect time, changes in time to first byte, and HTTP 429 or 5xx status codes. If these increase, hostload is adjusted and crawling slows down.
  <br><sub>`D1-C092` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D2-C024](D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-04`, `DEV-PRF-01`, the glossary term *Crawl rate limit (hostload)*</sub>

- **[Slide]** Crawl demand is driven by the quality of the site, the change frequency of its URLs and their popularity on the internet.
  <br><sub>`D1-C093` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D1-C377](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extended by [D1-C439](D1-S12-q-a.md) · Extended by [D2-C695](D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) · Extended by [D2-C709](D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) · Extended by [D3-C623](D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Used by the glossary term *Crawl demand*</sub>

- **[Slide]** If the quality or popularity of a URL is unknown, the aggregate quality or popularity of its parent path is used, then that path's parent, and so on.
  > "If quality or popularity is unknown, use parent root's aggregate quality or popularity is used, then, that path's parent's, and so on."
  <br><sub>`D1-C094` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D2-C369](D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) · Extended by [D2-C685](D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-10`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** New content inherits its starting crawl demand from the folder it sits in. Put new high-value content under sections Google already rates well, not under weak ones.
  <br><sub>`D1-C095` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · Extended by [D2-C686](D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-10`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Crawl budget was described as the attention span Google gives a website, and better performance increases it.
  <br><sub>`D1-C096` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D1-C373](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-PRF-01`, the glossary term *Crawl budget*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's crawl budget guide is written for sites with over 1 million unique pages that change weekly, over 10,000 pages that change daily, or many URLs reported as 'Discovered – currently not indexed'.
  <br><sub>`D1-C097` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · is the documentation · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D2-C706](D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** On smaller sites, slow indexing is almost always a demand problem, meaning quality, not a capacity problem.
  <br><sub>`D1-C098` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · Extended by [D2-C708](D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) · Extended by [D2-C714](D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) · Extended by [D2-C716](D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md)</sub>

- **[Slide]** Three things burn crawl budget: server errors unrelated to server load, useless pages and resources, and infinite URL spaces.
  <br><sub>`D1-C099` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D1-C378](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-08`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Six faceted-URL problems were shown: the same facets in a different order, irrelevant or conflicting facet combinations, excessive facet selection, facets on paginated series, facets combined with search queries, and optional facets with default values.
  <br><sub>`D1-C100` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Managing crawling of faceted navigation URLs](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/faceted-navigation) · Used by `DEV-URL-08`, the glossary term *Faceted navigation*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's faceted navigation guide prefers prevention: disallow filter URLs in robots.txt and keep crawlable only item pages plus one unfiltered listing page, or use URL fragments, which Google generally does not crawl. rel=canonical and nofollow are weaker, slower options.
  <br><sub>`D1-C101` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · is the documentation · [Managing crawling of faceted navigation URLs](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/faceted-navigation) · Extended by [D2-C188](D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Repeated by [D2-C284](D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-08`, the glossary term *Faceted navigation*</sub>

- **[Docs]** If faceted URLs must be crawled, use the standard & separator, keep filters in a consistent order, and return a 404 when a filter combination has no results.
  <br><sub>`D1-C102` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · is the documentation · [Managing crawling of faceted navigation URLs](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/faceted-navigation) · Extended by [D1-C404](D1-S11-lightning-session-c-crawling.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-09`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Four ways to manage crawl budget: use HTTP cache control, have good site navigation, restrict crawlers' access to faceted navigation and action URLs, and improve or remove useless content.
  <br><sub>`D1-C103` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D1-C379](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extended by [D2-C886](D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-08`, `DEV-URL-08`</sub>

- **[Docs]** HTTP caching for crawlers means supporting conditional requests (ETag with If-None-Match, or Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since) and answering 304 Not Modified when nothing changed. Google's crawling team has said it prefers ETag.
  <br><sub>`D1-C104` · Google, Search Central blog (9 December 2024) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · is the documentation · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget), [Crawling December: HTTP caching](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/12/crawling-december-caching) · Used by `DEV-SRV-08`</sub>

- **[Slide]** URLs disallowed through robots.txt do not affect crawl budget, because they are not fetched.
  <br><sub>`D1-C105` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D2-C021](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-02`, `F-025`</sub>

- **[Slide]** The noindex rule consumes crawl budget, because Google must fetch the page to see it.
  <br><sub>`D1-C106` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extended by [D2-C022](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C069](D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Extended by [D2-C697](D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-02`, `F-025`</sub>

- **[Slide]** The nofollow rule can still consume crawl budget: Google does not crawl through the nofollow link itself, but it still crawls the linked page when it finds that page through other links.
  <br><sub>`D1-C107` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [Qualify your outbound links to Google](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/qualify-outbound-links), [Managing crawling of faceted navigation URLs](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/faceted-navigation), [What Crawl Budget Means for Googlebot](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2017/01/what-crawl-budget-means-for-googlebot) · Used by `DEV-IDX-02`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google treats nofollow as a hint for crawling, not a block: nofollow links will generally not be followed, but the linked pages may still be crawled if Google finds them through sitemaps or other links. To stop Google fetching URLs on your own site, use a robots.txt disallow rule.
  <br><sub>`D1-C127` · Google Search Central, Search Central blog (10 September 2019) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · is the documentation · [Qualify your outbound links to Google](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/qualify-outbound-links), [Evolving "nofollow" – new ways to identify the nature of links](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2019/09/evolving-nofollow-new-ways-to-identify) · Extended by [D2-C067](D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-02`, `DEV-IDX-06`, the glossary term *nofollow*</sub>

- **[Slide]** The non-standard crawl-delay rule is not processed by Googlebot, so it does not save any crawl budget.
  <br><sub>`D1-C108` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Used by `DEV-IDX-02`, `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google advises against using noindex to save crawl budget and against using robots.txt to temporarily reallocate budget. Use robots.txt only for pages you never want crawled, and 404 or 410 for removed pages.
  <br><sub>`D1-C109` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · is the documentation · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Used by `DEV-ERR-01`, `DEV-IDX-02`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** A URL blocked in robots.txt can still be indexed without its content if other pages link to it, and Google cannot see a noindex on a page it is not allowed to fetch.
  <br><sub>`D1-C110` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · Extended by [D2-C020](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C846](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C849](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C058](D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Repeated by [D2-C850](D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Repeated by [D2-C851](D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guide to A/B testing says never to show one set of URLs to Googlebot and a different set to humans: that is cloaking, which is against Google's spam policies whether or not a test is running.
  <br><sub>`D1-C141` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · is the documentation · [Minimize A/B testing impact in Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/website-testing) · Used by `DEV-PRF-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Crawl budget is the finite amount of resources Google allocates to crawling a specific website, and it determines how many of the site's pages are discovered and how often they are revisited.
  <br><sub>`D1-C373` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget), [What Crawl Budget Means for Googlebot](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2017/01/what-crawl-budget-means-for-googlebot) · Extends [D1-C096](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by the glossary term *Crawl budget*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a proxy for how many requests per second the connection to a site can handle before Google hits the limit.
  <br><sub>`D1-C374` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extends [D1-C091](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extended by [D1-C546](D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-PRF-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Googlebot as a single standalone crawler is a historical idea: Google crawls through a centralised crawling infrastructure, so a request from a Google user agent in server logs is a request routed through that shared platform.
  <br><sub>`D1-C375` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post), [Crawling infrastructure](https://developers.google.com/crawling) · Extends [D1-C066](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extended by [D3-C624](D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Hostload applies per host, not necessarily per site: depending on how a site is configured, its CDN, its app, its subdomains and its main www host may be different hosts.
  <br><sub>`D1-C376` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extends [D1-C091](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-PRF-01`, the glossary term *Crawl rate limit (hostload)*</sub>

- **[Stage]** The quality that drives crawl demand is the quality of the site as a whole, not the quality of an individual page.
  <br><sub>`D1-C377` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C093](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extended by [D3-C623](D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google treats URLs that differ as different URLs and crawls all of them even when they lead to the same content, so infinite URL spaces such as calendars or many versions of a page burn crawl budget.
  <br><sub>`D1-C378` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [URL structure best practices for Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/url-structure), [What Crawl Budget Means for Googlebot](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2017/01/what-crawl-budget-means-for-googlebot) · Extends [D1-C099](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-08`, `DEV-URL-11`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The useless content worth improving or removing to save crawl budget includes very bad or low-quality pages, spam content, duplicate pages and soft error pages.
  <br><sub>`D1-C379` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [What Crawl Budget Means for Googlebot](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2017/01/what-crawl-budget-means-for-googlebot), [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extends [D1-C103](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** An audience member asked, in a question submitted before the event, whether crawl budget is still an SEO priority in 2026 or only relevant for very large sites.
  <br><sub>`D1-C380` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (audience member) · Answered by [D1-C381](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

  - **[Stage]** Not every site needs to worry about crawl budget, and this has always been so: a site with fewer than a few thousand URLs likely has no crawl budget problem, and a larger site does not necessarily have one either.
    <br><sub>`D1-C381` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [What Crawl Budget Means for Googlebot](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2017/01/what-crawl-budget-means-for-googlebot), [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget), [Crawl Stats report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9679690?hl=en) · Answers [D1-C380](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Repeated by [D1-C466](D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by the glossary term *Crawl budget*</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The stage rule of thumb (under a few thousand URLs crawl budget is unlikely to be a problem) and Google's crawl budget guide (D1-C097: sites with over a million pages that change about weekly, or over 10,000 pages that change daily) leave a middle range where a site should check Search Console's Crawl Stats report before blaming crawl budget for slow indexing.
  <br><sub>`D1-C382` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget</sub>

- **[Stage]** HTTP status codes do not all affect crawl budget in the same way, so knowing what each status code class does is one way to manage crawl budget.
  <br><sub>`D1-C383` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Every fetch that returns a 2xx success response consumes crawl budget.
  <br><sub>`D1-C384` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [What Crawl Budget Means for Googlebot](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2017/01/what-crawl-budget-means-for-googlebot) · Used by `DEV-SRV-08`</sub>

- **[Stage]** 4xx responses do not affect a site's crawl budget, because Google expects pages, content and products to come and go as a natural part of the web.
  <br><sub>`D1-C385` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes) · Repeats [D1-C072](D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) · Used by `DEV-ERR-01`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget matches Google's documentation that 4xx codes have no effect on crawl rate (D1-C072), with one exception: 429 Too Many Requests counts as a server error and slows crawling like a 5xx (D1-C071, D1-C092).
  <br><sub>`D1-C386` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget</sub>

- **[Stage]** An audience member asked, in questions submitted before the event, how often Googlebot should be expected to visit a site now that AI Mode has rolled out, and whether AI means more crawling.
  <br><sub>`D1-C387` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (audience member) · Answered by [D1-C388](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Answered by [D1-C389](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

  - **[Stage]** AI Mode is a feature that sits on top of Google's existing crawling infrastructure, so Google does not crawl a site more because of AI Mode.
    <br><sub>`D1-C388` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [AI features and your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features) · Answers [D1-C387](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extends [D1-C038](D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

  - **[Stage]** Google expects sites to see more crawling overall, because many other services, including AI services, now crawl the web besides Google.
    <br><sub>`D1-C389` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · Answers [D1-C387](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** An audience member asked, in a question submitted before the event, whether crawl frequency affects the ranking position of a URL.
  <br><sub>`D1-C390` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (audience member) · Answered by [D1-C391](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Answered by [D1-C392](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

  - **[Stage]** A higher crawl rate does not make a URL rank better; it only means Google checks the site more often.
    > "if your crawl rate is increased, that doesn't mean that you would rank better."
    <br><sub>`D1-C391` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [What Crawl Budget Means for Googlebot](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2017/01/what-crawl-budget-means-for-googlebot) · Answers [D1-C390](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

  - **[Stage]** Frequent crawling is usually a consequence, not a cause: Google visiting a site more often tends to signal that people are interested in the site and that its content is of high quality.
    <br><sub>`D1-C392` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Answers [D1-C390](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** To check whether a site has a crawl budget problem, use Search Console's crawl report (Crawl Stats), which breaks crawl requests down by response and by file type and shows crawl problems Google finds.
  <br><sub>`D1-C393` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [Crawl Stats report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9679690?hl=en) · Used by `DEV-MON-04`, the glossary term *Crawl Stats report*</sub>

- **[Stage]** The file-type breakdown of crawl requests in Search Console is useful for spotting anomalies, such as most crawling going to images on a site that has no images worth crawling.
  <br><sub>`D1-C394` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · consistent with Google docs · [Crawl Stats report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9679690?hl=en) · Used by `DEV-MON-04`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google advised checking crawl data in Search Console now and then without obsessing over crawl budget.
  <br><sub>`D1-C395` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Search Console's crawl data separates discovery (fetches of URLs Google has not seen before) from refresh (fetches of known URLs), and lets you drill down to the problematic URLs.
  <br><sub>`D1-C396` · Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [Crawl Stats report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9679690?hl=en) · Used by `DEV-MON-04`, `DEV-MON-11`, the glossary term *Crawl Stats report*</sub>

- **[Analysis]** A 404 fetch is still a fetch: Google's 2017 crawl budget post says generally any URL Googlebot crawls counts towards a site's crawl budget, so the stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget is best read as 'they do not slow crawling, and a 404 tells Google to crawl that URL less over time'.
  <br><sub>`D1-C419` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · [What Crawl Budget Means for Googlebot](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2017/01/what-crawl-budget-means-for-googlebot), [How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The stage remark that crawl demand follows the quality of the site as a whole sits beside the same talk's slide (D1-C094), which falls back to the parent path's aggregate only when a URL's own quality is unknown, and Google's crawl budget guide lists page quality among the demand factors; read it as site quality setting the baseline while known URL-level signals still count.
  <br><sub>`D1-C420` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget)</sub>
